text_summary.body: On 24 Shebat of Darius's second year Zechariah saw (1) a man on a red horse among myrtles with a patrol reporting the earth at rest, and heard the angel of the LORD plead for Jerusalem after "these seventy years" and the LORD promise to return with mercy and rebuild; (2) four horns that scattered Judah and four craftsmen to cast them down; (3) a man measuring Jerusalem, told that it would be unwalled for its multitude with the LORD as a wall of fire. An oracle calls the exiles to flee Babylon and promises the LORD's dwelling in Zion and the joining of many nations. (4) Joshua the high priest stood in filthy garments with the satan accusing him; the LORD rebuked the accuser, Joshua was cleansed and given charge of the house, and the LORD announced "my servant the Branch" and a stone with seven eyes. (5) A gold lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees; the word to Zerubbabel, "not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit"; his hands laid the foundation and will finish the house; the olive trees are two anointed ones. (6) A flying scroll, twenty by ten cubits, is the curse on thieves and false swearers. (7) Wickedness, a woman in an ephah under a lead cover, is carried by two winged women to the land of Shinar. (8) Four chariots with coloured horses, the four spirits of heaven, go out to the earth; those going north have quieted the LORD's spirit there.

setting.body: Mitchell dates 24 Shebat of Darius's second year to February 519. He doubts that the report "the whole earth rests" describes the empire at that date, given the revolts against Darius, and reads it otherwise.

constraints.textual_assertion: On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat, in the second year of Darius
assumptions: Babylonian Nisan-based regnal years: year 2 = 3 April 520 – 22 March 519 (Parker & Dubberstein). Shebat (month XI) fell in January–February 519; Mitchell gives "toward the middle of February" 519.

locations.role: "The daughter of Babylon" from which the exiles must flee (2:7)

terminology.term: the angel who talked with me
terminology.gloss: The interpreting angel of the night visions, distinct in the text from the angel of the LORD (1:9, 11–12).
Persons associated with oil — those anointed for office (Mitchell; Keil: "endowed or supplied with oil").
With the article: "the adversary", the accusing figure in the heavenly court (cf. Job 1–2).
A dry measure (about a bushel) and the basket of that size; with the lead weight an image of commerce (Guzik).

competing_reconstructions.label: "These seventy years" (1:12): from the destruction of 587/586 to Darius's second year
proponents: C. F. Keil (1868), after Vitringa and Hengstenberg: the seventy years were "completed twice"
competing_reconstructions.summary: Jeremiah's seventy years had ended under Cyrus, but nearly seventy years had also passed since the Temple's destruction while it still lay in ruins.

competing_reconstructions.label: "These seventy years" counted from 605 or loosely
competing_reconstructions.summary: Either from the date of Jeremiah's prophecy (605) or by inadvertently including the years since the fall of Babylon.

competing_reconstructions.label: The man among the myrtles
proponents: D. Guzik: the Angel of the LORD, a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ
C. F. Keil: the angel of Jehovah, of one essence with Jehovah
competing_reconstructions.summary: Theological identifications; the text calls him the angel of the LORD (1:11).

competing_reconstructions.label: The Branch (3:8): the Messiah or Zerubbabel
proponents: C. F. Keil (1868); D. Guzik: the Messiah
H. G. Mitchell (1912), after Marti: Zerubbabel, with 3:8b a gloss
competing_reconstructions.summary: See the prophecy record "my servant the Branch".

competing_reconstructions.label: Zech 4:9 and the date of the foundation
proponents: Read with Ezra 3:8–10 (536) or with Hag 2:18 (520) — see the Ezra 3 foundation event
competing_reconstructions.summary: "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation" names Zerubbabel, not Sheshbazzar (Ezra 5:16).

competing_reconstructions.label: The four chariots (6:1–8)
proponents: Some commentators: Daniel's four empires (rejected by Keil and by Guzik)
D. Guzik: angelic agents of judgment, like the horsemen of Rev 6
competing_reconstructions.summary: Keil: neither the number nor the colours point to Daniel's monarchies.

commentary.paraphrase: Guzik reads the horsemen as an imperial-style patrol and the horns, if read prophetically, as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome.
Guzik sees a short-term fulfilment of 2:1–5 under Ezra and Nehemiah and an ultimate one under the Messiah.
